body:
Meaning of remote sensing

Remote sensing is the science of obtaining information about an object, area or phenomenon without making direct physical contact with it. In geography, it is primarily used to study the Earth's surface, atmosphere, oceans and natural resources by recording electromagnetic radiation reflected, emitted or scattered by them.

A satellite observing agricultural fields, an aircraft photographing a forest and a weather satellite recording the development of a cyclone are examples of remote sensing.

Remote sensing: The acquisition and interpretation of information about an object or phenomenon from a distance, without direct physical contact.

Platform and sensor

A sensor is an instrument that detects and records electromagnetic radiation. A platform is the structure or vehicle on which the sensor is mounted.

PlatformExamplesTypical application
Ground-basedTripods, observation towersDetailed local observations
AirborneAircraft, helicopters, dronesLocal and regional mapping
SpaceborneArtificial satellitesRegional and global observations

A satellite is therefore a platform, whereas a camera, radiometer or radar instrument carried by it is a sensor. Remote sensing is not restricted to satellites.

Stages of remote sensing

  1. Energy source: Electromagnetic energy originates from the Sun, the observed object itself or an artificial source carried by the sensor.
  2. Atmospheric interaction: Radiation passing through the atmosphere may undergo scattering or absorption.
  3. Interaction with the target: The target reflects, absorbs, transmits or scatters incoming radiation. It may also emit radiation according to its temperature.
  4. Detection: A sensor records radiation reaching it from the target.
  5. Data transmission and processing: Recorded measurements are transmitted or transferred for correction and processing into usable images or other data products.
  6. Interpretation: Features such as vegetation, water bodies, settlements and geological formations are identified from the recorded information.
  7. Application: The interpreted information is used to prepare maps, monitor changes and support geographical decisions.

Advantages and limitations

Remote sensing enables observation of extensive, inaccessible or hazardous regions. Repeated observations make it possible to study changes in vegetation, coastlines, glaciers, settlements and water bodies over time.

However, a sensor records electromagnetic signals rather than directly identifying every object or geographical process. Interpretation is necessary to convert those signals into meaningful information.

Ground truth refers to reference information obtained through field observations or other reliable direct measurements. It is used to interpret and validate remote sensing results. Remote sensing reduces the need for extensive fieldwork but does not eliminate it.

Prelims focus

  • Remote sensing obtains information without direct physical contact.
  • A platform carries a sensor; a sensor detects radiation.
  • Remote sensing may be ground-based, airborne or spaceborne.
  • Repeated observations support geographical change detection.
  • Ground truth helps validate image interpretation.
  • Trap: Remote sensing does not necessarily require a satellite.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Practical Work in Geography, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 6, Introduction to Remote Sensing, pp. 69–75; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 11, Geography, 2020 reprint, Chapter 16, Geographical Information and Map Making, pp. 121–122; NASA Earth Observatory, Remote Sensing. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Electromagnetic radiation

Electromagnetic radiation is energy that travels in the form of electromagnetic waves. Unlike sound waves, electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium and can travel through a vacuum.

Electromagnetic waves are characterised by their wavelength and frequency. Wavelength is the distance between successive corresponding points of a wave, while frequency is the number of wave cycles passing a point per second.

Wavelength and frequency are inversely related. Longer wavelengths correspond to lower frequencies, while shorter wavelengths correspond to higher frequencies.

The electromagnetic spectrum

The complete range of electromagnetic radiation, arranged according to wavelength or frequency, is called the electromagnetic spectrum.

From shorter to longer wavelengths, its principal regions are gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet radiation, visible light, infrared radiation and radio waves. Microwaves occupy a portion of the radio-wave region and are commonly treated as a separate category in remote sensing because of their distinctive applications.

Important regions in remote sensing

Spectral regionImportant characteristicApplication
Visible lightApproximately 0.4–0.7 micrometresLand cover, natural-colour imagery
Near-infraredStrong reflection by healthy vegetationVegetation and water discrimination
Shortwave infraredSensitive to moisture differencesVegetation moisture, minerals, snow discrimination
Thermal infraredRadiation emitted by objectsSurface temperature, thermal anomalies
MicrowaveLonger wavelengths than infraredRadar imaging, soil moisture, ocean observations

Visible light constitutes only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Remote sensing instruments can record radiation that the human eye cannot detect.

Interaction of radiation with Earth's surface

When electromagnetic radiation reaches an object, some energy may be reflected, some absorbed and some transmitted through the material. The relative proportions depend on the wavelength and the properties of the object.

  • Reflection: Radiation returns from the surface of an object.
  • Absorption: Energy is taken up by the material.
  • Transmission: Radiation passes through the material.
  • Emission: An object releases electromagnetic radiation, including thermal radiation associated with its temperature.

Spectral signature

A spectral signature is the characteristic pattern of electromagnetic radiation reflected or emitted by a material across different wavelengths. Different surface materials can often be distinguished because their spectral responses are different.

Vegetation, water and soil

Healthy green vegetation absorbs much of the red and blue visible light because of photosynthetic pigments such as chlorophyll. It reflects more green light than red or blue light, giving leaves their familiar green appearance. The internal structure of healthy leaves produces relatively strong reflection in the near-infrared region.

Water generally absorbs near-infrared radiation strongly and consequently appears dark in many near-infrared images. Its appearance in visible wavelengths can vary with depth, suspended sediment and other substances.

Bare soil has a spectral response that varies with mineral composition, organic matter, surface roughness and moisture. Moist soil generally reflects less radiation than comparable dry soil in several optical wavelengths.

Atmospheric windows

The atmosphere does not transmit every wavelength equally. Gases such as ozone, water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb radiation in particular wavelength ranges. Atmospheric particles also scatter radiation.

Wavelength ranges through which radiation passes relatively freely are called atmospheric windows. Many remote sensing instruments are designed to operate within these windows so that radiation from the Earth's surface can reach the sensor.

Atmospheric windows are ranges of electromagnetic wavelengths with relatively high atmospheric transmission. They are not physical openings in the atmosphere.

Prelims focus

  • Longer wavelength corresponds to lower frequency.
  • Visible light occupies approximately 0.4–0.7 micrometres.
  • Healthy vegetation strongly reflects near-infrared radiation.
  • Water generally absorbs near-infrared radiation strongly.
  • Thermal infrared observations help estimate surface temperature.
  • Atmospheric windows permit relatively efficient transmission of radiation.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Practical Work in Geography, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 6, Introduction to Remote Sensing, pp. 71–75; NASA Earth Observatory, Remote Sensing, sections on the electromagnetic spectrum and atmospheric transmission. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Classification according to energy source

Remote sensing instruments are classified as active or passive according to whether they provide their own energy to illuminate the target.

Passive remote sensing

A passive sensor detects naturally available radiation. It does not transmit its own energy towards the target for measurement.

Many passive optical instruments record sunlight reflected from the Earth's surface. These instruments depend on solar illumination and generally cannot obtain ordinary reflected-light images at night.

However, passive sensors do not always depend on sunlight. Thermal infrared sensors detect naturally emitted radiation and can operate during both day and night. Passive microwave radiometers can also record naturally emitted microwave radiation.

Active remote sensing

An active sensor transmits its own electromagnetic energy towards a target and measures the returned signal. It can operate independently of natural illumination.

Radar, or Radio Detection and Ranging, transmits microwave signals and records the returned energy. Many radar systems can observe the Earth's surface through cloud cover and during darkness. The returned signal depends on factors such as surface roughness, moisture and the properties of the target.

LiDAR, or Light Detection and Ranging, transmits laser pulses. It is used to obtain information about surface elevation, terrain and vegetation height. Unlike microwave radar, conventional LiDAR cannot reliably observe the ground through thick clouds.

Active and passive sensing are distinguished by the source of the measured energy, not simply by whether the sensor operates during daytime or nighttime. Thermal infrared sensing is commonly passive even though it can operate at night.

Optical and microwave remote sensing

Optical remote sensing commonly uses visible and infrared wavelengths. Reflected-light optical imagery is useful for identifying vegetation, water and land cover, but clouds can obstruct the view of the Earth's surface.

Microwave remote sensing includes both active radar instruments and passive microwave radiometers. Many microwave wavelengths can pass through clouds more effectively than visible light. This makes microwave observations particularly valuable during cyclones and floods.

Cloud penetration does not imply unlimited penetration through every material. Heavy precipitation and the wavelength used can affect microwave measurements.

Satellite orbits

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite moves in a circular orbit above the Equator, in the direction of Earth's rotation, at an altitude of approximately 36,000 km. Its orbital period equals the Earth's rotation period relative to the stars, approximately 24 hours.

It appears stationary relative to a fixed point on the Earth's surface. It can therefore repeatedly observe a broad region without waiting for successive orbital passes. This property is particularly useful for monitoring cloud systems, cyclones and rapidly changing weather.

Polar and near-polar orbits

Polar-orbiting satellites travel approximately in a north–south direction and pass near the poles. As the Earth rotates beneath their orbital paths, they observe successive strips of its surface.

Many Earth observation satellites operate in Sun-synchronous orbits, which are usually near-polar orbits arranged to cross a given latitude at approximately the same local solar time on corresponding passes. Similar illumination conditions help compare images recorded on different dates.

The width of the ground strip observed during a satellite pass is called the swath width.

FeatureGeostationary orbitTypical near-polar orbit
Ground observationBroad, approximately fixed regionSuccessive strips of Earth's surface
Observation frequencyFrequent observations of the same regionRepeated passes after an interval
Typical applicationWeather monitoringLand resources and detailed mapping

These are common applications, not exclusive rules. Actual image detail and observation frequency depend on the sensor and satellite mission design.

Prelims focus

  • Active sensors transmit energy; passive sensors detect naturally available radiation.
  • Radar uses microwaves, whereas LiDAR uses laser pulses.
  • Passive thermal sensors can operate at night.
  • A geostationary satellite appears fixed above the Equator.
  • Sun-synchronous observations provide approximately consistent local solar times.
  • Trap: Microwave sensing is not necessarily active sensing.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Practical Work in Geography, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 6, Introduction to Remote Sensing, pp. 74–81; NASA Earth Observatory, Remote Sensing, active and passive remote sensing sections; NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training, Fundamentals of Remote Sensing, 2023. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
